clue.text: One gets jumpy being on the spot with this

definitions.text: One gets jumpy being on the spot with this

blocks.clueFragment: One gets jumpy being on the spot
blocks.note: surface reading: someone nervous after being put on the spot
setter's reading: a child jumping up and down in one place with a piece of playground kit

explanation.surface: Someone grows nervous when put on the spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumpy' and 'on the spot' read as nerves, but taken literally they describe hopping in one place.
explanation.definitionFit: A child using this playground cord hops repeatedly without moving forward, literally jumping in place.

clue.text: Undertaker at a christen-ins?

blocks.note: surface reading: a funeral director, oddly placed at a baptism
setter's reading: one who undertakes promises on a baby's behalf at a christening

explanation.surface: A funeral director turns up at a christening party.
explanation.walkthrough: An undertaker here is simply someone who undertakes a duty; at a baptism the godparent makes vows for the child.
explanation.definitionFit: A godparent is formally called a sponsor, pledging at baptism to guide the child's religious upbringing.

clue.text: The last thing to do to Polonius

definitions.text: The last thing to do to Polonius

blocks.note: surface reading: a final task on a list
setter's reading: what must finally be done with the body of the old courtier Hamlet stabs

explanation.surface: A final job to be done concerning Hamlet's Polonius.
explanation.walkthrough: Polonius is killed behind the arras in Hamlet, and Hamlet lugs the body away; the last thing to do with a corpse is burial.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter means to bury a body in a grave, the final rite owed to the dead.

clue.text: Bob hangs on to this

blocks.note: surface reading: a man called Bob
setter's reading: a bob is the lead weight suspended from a builder's cord

explanation.surface: A man named Bob clings on to something.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob looks like a name, but a bob is the weight at the end of a cord used to find the vertical.
explanation.definitionFit: Builders use a weighted cord to check walls are truly vertical; the weight on its end is called a bob.

clue.text: Head witness lacks sense

indicators.note: something that lacks a part has had that part taken away, so letters are removed

blocks.note: taken as written
wit is good sense or understanding; the backwards run of letters across 'lacks sense' is a coincidence, not the setter's device

explanation.surface: A senior witness in court shows no sense.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking WIT from the front of WITNESS leaves NESS. 'Head' looks like a chief, but here it is a geographical feature.
explanation.definitionFit: A ness is a headland or promontory, as in Loch Ness's neighbouring place names and Dungeness on the Kent coast.

clue.text: Girl named in a Lords amendment

indicators.note: an amendment alters wording, so the given letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl is mentioned by name in a House of Lords amendment.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosalind is a female first name, famously the heroine of Shakespeare's As You Like It.

clue.text: Vocation Frederic missed at Penzance

blocks.note: surface reading: a career someone failed to follow
setter's reading: in The Pirates of Penzance, Frederic's nurse misheard his intended trade and apprenticed him to a pirate

explanation.surface: A young man named Frederic misses out on his calling in a Cornish town.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's The Pirates of Penzance, the hard-of-hearing nursemaid Ruth confused two similar-sounding trades.
explanation.definitionFit: Frederic's father wanted him to be a ship's guide steering vessels into harbour, the job he never got.

clue.text: Gets worried about feature pictures

indicators.note: worried means disturbed or pulled about, so the letters are jumbled
about means going around, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: taken as written
the chin is one of the features of the face

explanation.surface: Someone is anxious about a feature with pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feature' suggests a magazine article, but it is a part of the face.
explanation.definitionFit: Etchings are prints made from engraved metal plates, a kind of picture.

clue.text: One should easily get versed in this system

definitions.text: One should easily get versed in this system

blocks.note: surface reading: anyone should quickly become familiar with it
setter's reading: versed as in written in verse, and the decimal measuring system is simple to learn

explanation.surface: Anyone should find this system easy to master.
explanation.walkthrough: The word describes both the decimal system of measures and poetry written in regular rhythm, so 'versed' does double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: The metre-based measuring system works in tens, and verse built on regular rhythm is described with the same adjective.

clue.text: Angry demonstrations at Hatch End?

blocks.note: surface reading: protests or fits of temper
setter's reading: Hatch End is a London suburb, but at the end of hatching the chick breaks free of the egg

explanation.surface: Furious protests break out in the north London suburb of Hatch End.
explanation.walkthrough: Hatch End is a real place in north-west London; read as two words, it is the moment an egg hatches and the chick emerges.
explanation.definitionFit: Sudden explosions of anger are called by this word, which also describes the chick emerging from its shell.

clue.text: The French and 'English meet at the river

blocks.note: le is French for the
the same word in English, which is just the

explanation.surface: A Frenchman and an Englishman meet by a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The French and English' means the word 'the' in French followed by the word 'the' in English.
explanation.definitionFit: Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in the Greek underworld, whose waters wiped out the memories of the dead.

clue.text: Writer whose quarters include bed for baby

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: south and east, two of the four compass quarters
a crib is a baby's cot

explanation.surface: An author whose rooms contain a cot for an infant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quarters' looks like lodgings, but it means compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: A scribe is someone who writes, originally a copyist of manuscripts.

clue.text: Alias Arrowsmith

blocks.note: surface reading: another name used by someone
setter's reading: a surname meaning a maker of arrows, which has an equivalent trade surname

explanation.surface: A person going under the name Arrowsmith.
explanation.walkthrough: Arrowsmith looks like a person's name; read as a job, it is someone who makes arrows, which is another trade surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A fletcher is a craftsman who makes and feathers arrows, and is also a common English surname.

clue.text: He doesn't mind getting in a hole, especially if a golfer!

definitions.text: He doesn't mind getting in a hole

blocks.clueFragment: He doesn't mind getting in a hole
blocks.note: first meaning: a burrowing animal happy underground
second meaning: slang for a weak or novice player of a game

explanation.surface: Someone untroubled by trouble, particularly a golfer stuck in a bunker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a hole' sounds like being in difficulties; on a golf course a hole is where the ball should go.
explanation.definitionFit: This burrowing animal lives in warrens dug underground, and the same word is British slang for a poor or amateur sports player.

clue.text: The limit of advancement in service

definitions.text: The limit of advancement in service

blocks.note: surface reading: how far someone can be promoted
setter's reading: in tennis, a server may not step over the back line of the court

explanation.surface: How far one may rise in a career of service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advancement in service' reads as promotion, but in tennis the server must stay behind the court's end line.
explanation.definitionFit: The baseline is the line at each end of a tennis court; a server who steps over it commits a foot fault.

clue.text: One device the elephant trainer shouldn't need

definitions.text: One device the elephant trainer shouldn't need

blocks.note: surface reading: a gadget or tool
setter's reading: an elephant never forgets, so its trainer need not help it remember

explanation.surface: A tool that a circus elephant's handler can do without.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb says an elephant never forgets, so no aid to memory should be needed.
explanation.definitionFit: A mnemonic is a memory aid such as a rhyme or acronym that helps one recall facts.

clue.text: No astronaut, but seemed crazy about lunar research !

definitions.text: No astronaut, but seemed crazy about lunar research !

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who never went into space

blocks.clueFragment: but seemed crazy about lunar research !
blocks.note: setter's reading: a Wiltshire yokel caught raking a pond for the reflected moon

explanation.surface: A person who never went to space yet seemed obsessed with studying the moon.
explanation.walkthrough: Legend says Wiltshire smugglers raking a pond for hidden brandy told excisemen they were trying to rake out the moon, and were dismissed as simpletons.
explanation.definitionFit: Moonraker is the nickname for a native of Wiltshire, after a folk tale of villagers raking for the moon.

clue.text: A long boat, grotesque and huge

blocks.note: a gig is a light, narrow rowing boat
antic is an old adjective for grotesque or bizarre

explanation.surface: An enormous, weird-looking longboat.
explanation.definitionFit: Gigantic means of enormous size, like a giant.

clue.text: This year could produce wild excitement

indicators.note: these words promise something made from the material, so the letters are reworked into a new word

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The coming twelve months may bring frenzied excitement.
explanation.definitionFit: Hysteria is an uncontrolled outburst of emotion, a state of frenzied agitation.

clue.text: She commended the witches in Macbeth

definitions.text: She commended the witches in Macbeth

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman giving praise
setter's reading: the goddess of witchcraft who says 'I commend your pains' to the three witches

explanation.surface: A woman praises the three witches in Shakespeare's Scottish play.
explanation.walkthrough: In Act IV of Macbeth, the goddess of witchcraft arrives and congratulates the witches on their work.
explanation.definitionFit: Hecate is the Greek goddess of magic and witchcraft, who appears as the witches' mistress in Macbeth.

clue.text: One's in the Opposition, from what we bear

definitions.text: One's in the Opposition, from what we bear

blocks.note: surface reading: a politician on the benches facing the government
setter's reading: things we suffer, whose opposite in a business account is profits

explanation.surface: Someone sits in Parliament's Opposition, judging by what we must endure.
explanation.walkthrough: Profit and loss stand opposed in the accounts, so this is the opposite column; it is also something people must bear.
explanation.definitionFit: Losses are things suffered or endured, and they stand opposite profits on a balance sheet.

clue.text: Fields of activity for all rounders?

blocks.note: first meaning: areas of interest or influence
second meaning: perfectly round solid objects, round in every direction

explanation.surface: Areas of the game suited to cricketers who both bat and bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: An all-rounder in cricket is a player good at both batting and bowling; here it means something round all over.
explanation.definitionFit: A sphere is a domain of activity, and also the geometric solid that is round in every direction.

clue.text: Huge deficiency in some fuel

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: coal is a fuel
a loss is a shortfall or deficiency

explanation.surface: An enormous shortage in a supply of fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: Colossal means immense, like the Colossus, the giant statue at Rhodes.

clue.text: Tonic for vocalists

blocks.note: surface reading: a medicine or pick-me-up
setter's reading: the tonic system of naming notes do, re, mi, used to teach singing

explanation.surface: A pick-me-up for singers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tonic' sounds like a restorative, but tonic sol-fa is the method of naming scale notes do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti.
explanation.definitionFit: Sol-fa is the system of syllables for musical notes used in teaching singers to sight-read.

clue.text: “ Beware the pine-tree's withered ” (Longfellow)

blocks.note: surface reading: a line of verse with a word missing
setter's reading: complete the quotation from Longfellow's poem Excelsior

explanation.surface: A warning line from a Longfellow poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The line from Excelsior runs 'Beware the pine-tree's withered branch! Beware the awful avalanche!'
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word completes the old man's warning to the youth climbing the mountain in Longfellow's poem.

clue.text: Money in music ?

blocks.note: first meaning: paper currency, banknotes
second meaning: the individual sounds written on a stave

explanation.surface: There's cash to be made in the music business.
explanation.definitionFit: Paper money comes as banknotes, and a melody is made of individual pitched sounds written on a stave.

clue.text: Hidden in the straw is probably this

definitions.text: Hidden in the straw is probably this

indicators.note: hidden in says the letters lie concealed inside the following words

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the end of straw and the start of the next two words

explanation.surface: Something small is probably lurking in the straw.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines: a small tuft is what you would expect to find in straw.
explanation.definitionFit: A wisp is a small thin bunch of straw or hay, so it is what straw holds.

clue.text: Of sound quality

blocks.note: surface reading: of reliable or solid standard
setter's reading: relating to the quality of a sound or tone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound quality' reads as 'good quality', but sound here means audio.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonal describes anything relating to tone, the character or pitch of a musical sound.

clue.text: A cheat at cards?

blocks.note: surface reading: a swindler
setter's reading: a player who wins tricks in a card game such as bridge or whist

explanation.surface: A card sharp.
explanation.walkthrough: In card games a trick is one round of play, so a trick-taker is just a winning player, not a dishonest one.
explanation.definitionFit: A trickster is a swindler or deceiver, and at cards the word can be read as someone who takes tricks.

clue.text: Slogans such as “ Stop chief ” and ” A fair top ”?

definitions.text: Slogans such as “ Stop chief ” and ” A fair top ”?

blocks.note: surface reading: examples of popular sayings

blocks.clueFragment: “ Stop chief ” and ” A fair top ”?
blocks.note: setter's reading: stop and catch are synonyms, and these are wordplay phrases each hiding a catch

explanation.surface: Popular sayings given as examples of slogans.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted phrases are odd jokes rather than real slogans; the solver is meant to read them as phrases built around a catch, a trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Catchphrases are well-known slogans or sayings repeated so often they become identified with someone.
